Betting Basics

Common Sports Betting Mistakes Beginners Make

Published October 27, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Most new bettors don't lose because they're bad at picking winners. Plenty of break-even or slightly-below-break-even handicappers still bleed their bankroll dry over a season, because the leak isn't in the picks — it's in the habits around them. The seven mistakes below show up constantly in beginner betting patterns, and each one has a specific, fixable mechanism behind it rather than just "bet smarter."

In this guide

  1. Betting by feel instead of by unit size
  2. Stacking too many legs into a parlay
  3. Never shopping for a better price
  4. Betting with your fandom instead of your head
  5. Raising your bet size to chase a loss
  6. Never checking your bets against the closing line
  7. Treating a stranger's "lock of the day" as a sure thing

Betting by feel instead of by unit size

A beginner's bet sizes are usually driven by how confident a pick feels that day — $20 on a coin-flip game, $150 on a "can't lose" primetime favorite. The problem is that confidence and actual edge are two different things, and sizing off the first one means a single bad week on your most-confident bets can erase a month of smaller, disciplined wins. A standard fix is flat unit sizing: pick one unit size equal to roughly 1-3% of your total bankroll, and bet in multiples of that unit based on how strong you genuinely believe your edge is — not how good the game feels. On a $1,000 bankroll, a 2% unit is $20; a bet you feel very strongly about might be 2 units ($40), never 10 units ($200) just because it's Sunday night. Our full bankroll management guide walks through sizing in more detail.

Stacking too many legs into a parlay

Parlays aren't a mistake by themselves — they're a legitimate, if high-variance, bet type. The mistake is not understanding how fast the vig compounds as legs get added, because a sportsbook builds a parlay's payout by multiplying each leg's own decimal odds together, and each of those legs already has its own built-in margin.

Legs (each -110)Parlay payout on $100Chance to hit (true 50/50 legs)Expected result on $100
1$190.9150%-$4.55
3$695.7912.5%-$13.03
5$2,535.903.125%-$20.75

That middle column is the one that gets beginners — a five-leg parlay can look like a modest $25 bet to win roughly $609 in profit, which doesn't sound reckless until you realize the true chance of hitting all five coin-flip-type legs is roughly 1 in 32. The expected loss as a share of your stake grows with every leg you add, because you're compounding a small per-leg disadvantage five separate times rather than once. None of this means never parlay; it means treating parlays as the long-shot, high-variance side of your betting rather than your default bet type, and understanding how correlation changes the math when the legs come from the same game.

Never shopping for a better price

The same side of the same game is rarely priced identically across every sportsbook. One book might have a favorite at -115 while another has it at -108 — a small gap on paper, but one that compounds across a season of betting into a meaningfully different outcome, the same way a few extra basis points of interest compounds on a savings account. A beginner who only ever opens one app is paying that gap on every single bet without ever seeing it. See our line shopping guide for how much this actually adds up to over a season of regular betting.

Betting with your fandom instead of your head

Betting on — or against — your own favorite team is one of the fastest ways to let emotion override a real edge. The tell is usually in the inconsistency: a fan who'd never bet their team as a 9-point underdog against a division rival will happily bet them as a 3-point favorite the very next week, even if the second bet is objectively the worse number. A simple guardrail that works for a lot of bettors: either stop betting your own team's games entirely, or write down what you'd bet if you had zero emotional stake in the outcome, then compare that number to what you actually want to bet before placing it.

Raising your bet size to chase a loss

Losing a bet doesn't change the true odds of the next one, but it changes how a lot of bettors behave — the instinct to size up on the next game "to get back to even" turns one ordinary losing day into a much bigger one if the second bet also loses. This is the single most damaging habit in recreational betting, and it's common enough that it has its own dedicated guide on guardrails worth building against it: see chasing losses and how to build guardrails for specific tactics, including hard daily stop-losses and pre-committing to your unit size before you know the day's results.

Never checking your bets against the closing line

Most beginners track only whether a bet won or lost. Sharper bettors also track where the line closed relative to where they bet it — a concept called closing line value. If you consistently bet a favorite at -3 and the line closes at -4.5, you were getting a better number than the market settled on, which is a sign of real process even on bets that happen to lose. Beginners who skip this entirely have no way to tell whether a losing month reflects bad luck on sound bets or a genuinely bad process, because results alone take a large sample size to separate from variance. Read more in our closing line value guide.

Treating a stranger's "lock of the day" as a sure thing

Social media and betting forums are full of accounts posting a daily "lock" with screenshots of past wins and no visible record of the losses. There's no regulatory requirement that a tout disclose a full, verifiable record, and a recommendation that's framed as certain is a marketing choice, not a reflection of actual win probability — even a legitimately well-researched pick is still just one side of a two-sided market the sportsbook itself thinks is close enough to take action on both sides of. Treat any outside pick the same way you'd treat your own: with a unit size that reflects genuine uncertainty, never a bet size that assumes it can't lose.

The pattern underneath all seven: almost every one of these mistakes comes down to a gap between how confident a bet feels and how much it's actually supported by a process you could explain to someone else. Closing that gap, more than finding better picks, is what separates bettors who are still playing with their original bankroll a year later from the ones who aren't.

If you're just getting started, it's worth working backward through a few of our foundational guides first: how odds work, every common bet type, and how the vig affects your real break-even win rate — all three show up, directly or indirectly, in most of the mistakes above.

Frequently asked questions

What's the single most common mistake new bettors make?

Sizing bets off how confident a pick feels rather than a consistent unit size tied to bankroll. It's less dramatic than chasing losses or over-parlaying, but it's the most common because it happens on nearly every bet, not just the bad days.

Are parlays always a bad bet?

Not inherently — they're a legitimate higher-variance bet type that can be fun and occasionally profitable. The mistake is using them as a primary strategy without understanding how much the vig compounds as legs are added, which the table above shows directly.

How much should a beginner bet per game?

A common starting point is 1-3% of your total bankroll per standard-confidence bet, adjusted up or down slightly based on genuine conviction — never doubled or tripled just to chase a prior loss back.

Does it matter which sportsbook I use if the odds look similar?

Yes, over time. Small per-bet price differences of a few cents compound across a season of regular betting into a real difference in results, which is why many consistent bettors maintain accounts at more than one book specifically to shop for the better number.

Is tracking closing line value really necessary for a casual bettor?

It's optional for someone betting purely for entertainment, but it's the most reliable way to evaluate your own process over a sample too small to judge by results alone — a few months of losses on bets that consistently beat the closing number is a very different signal than a few months of losses on bets that didn't.
